summary.en: The United States has revived a torture indictment against Maduro for ordering torture of rivals and deployed Space Force electromagnetic and electronic warfare systems against Venezuela while pressuring Reliance to refine Venezuelan oil. CIA Director Ratcliffe visited Havana accompanied by a paramilitary operative linked to the operation that killed 32 Cuban soldiers, and he is now shifting focus from Maduro’s capture to Cuba. Opposition leader María Corina Machado has returned to Venezuela after months in exile, prompting nationwide protests demanding elections and her return. The Pentagon has banned DoD personnel from using nonpublic information to bet on U.S. military actions involving Venezuela, and the U.S. Embassy has reopened to full staff, while UCDP recorded 2 battle-related deaths in 2007.
summary.nb: USA har gjenopptatt en torturanklage mot Maduro for å ha beordret tortur av rivaler og har satt i drift elektromagnetiske og elektroniske krigssystemer fra Space Force mot Venezuela mens de presser Reliance til å raffinere venezuelansk olje. CIA-direktør Ratcliffe besøkte Havanna sammen med en paramilitær operativ knyttet til operasjonen som drepte 32 kubanske soldater, og han skifter nå fokus fra å fange Maduro til Cuba. Opposisjonslederen María Corina Machado har kommet tilbake til Venezuela etter måneder i eksil, noe som har utløst landsomfattende protester som krever valg og hennes retur. Pentagon har forbudt DoD-personell å bruke ikke-offentlig informasjon til å satse på amerikanske militære handlinger mot Venezuela, og den amerikanske ambassaden har åpnet igjen med fullt personale, mens UCDP registrerte 2 dødsfall knyttet til kamper i 2007.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro and Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
